bull.b: GE Aerospace benefits from a large installed base and long engine life cycles that create recurring maintenance, parts and support demand. This aftermarket exposure can provide durable revenue visibility and typically supports stronger economics than relying only on new-engine deliveries.

Raised revenue guidance and a backlog exceeding $170 billion indicate strong demand visibility across commercial and defense propulsion. The combination of current growth and contracted future work supports sustained capacity utilization, investment planning and earnings momentum over the coming quarters.

Strong operating cash flow and high free-cash-flow conversion suggest that reported earnings are translating effectively into liquidity. This supports continued research, capital investment, customer support and shareholder or balance-sheet actions without depending entirely on external financing.

bear.b: Debt modestly exceeding equity and a lower equity base reduce financial flexibility relative to lower-leverage peers. If earnings weaken, this structure could make it harder to absorb volatility, fund expansion internally or allocate capital while maintaining comfortable financial resilience.

The expected GE9X headwind could weigh on profit growth even as shipment volumes rise. Certification timing and higher volume-related costs create a multi-quarter earnings drag, making margin expansion less certain and increasing dependence on services and other programs to offset it.

Higher spare-parts delinquency and slower conversion of services orders into revenue can pressure working capital, cash timing and operational execution. These issues may limit the benefit of strong demand in the near term and require sustained management attention to restore reliable delivery.
